title: [AINews] Google admits AI Mode hurts Search revenue; -15% $500B drop worst since 2004 IPO. AI Bear Market coming?
summary:
As an engineer-focused newsletter we only very rarely let financial stories through (our last example was Jan 2025 ), but when this is about the future of Google and Google Search , with a recently departed AI leadership, you cannot not care. 

 At its heart is the tension between overview pages and underlying pages they summarize. Any good enough summary obviates the need for you reading the source. Google’s Featured Snippets or Knowledge Panels have long had that tension with the publishers that supply that data. But now, Google’s own AI Overviews are potentially affecting traffic with… Google's Search revenue. 

 Google doesn’t break out AI Mode in sufficient detail that we can make any sort of rigorous analysis, but most people are quoting Philipp Schindler (Chief Business Officer): 

 “It’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.” 

 Together with other bad earnings results it set off a range of steep declines throughout tech: 

 View post on X ↗ 

 This is against a backdrop of souring tech/AI sentiment in public markets - and with OpenAI raising at $1.25T not $1.4T , not the sort of thing you want in the lead up to one of the biggest tech IPOs of all time. 

 View post on X ↗ 

 AI News for 10/29/2026-10/30/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space .

title: dbreunig/nesformer
summary:
dbreunig/nesformer 

Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen!

 In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system:

 Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed. 

 Followed by:

 I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. 

 Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow.

 Via Hacker News 

 Tags: games , ai , generative-ai , llms , drew-breunig , qwen , conformance-suites

title: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks?
summary:
Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and GitLab, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance . The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks , so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this.
 The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained , which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid.

 A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand.

title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
summary:
At a glance 

 Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.

 To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings.

 The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss.

 Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material.

 Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly.
